Trap: pricing only usable area makes B look $50,400 cheaper ($504,000 vs. $453,600), and marking usable area up by 20% and 30% applies the factors to usable instead of rentable area, making B look $15,120 cheaper ($604,800 vs. $589,680).
citation: DOS Salesperson Syllabus Subject 16 (loss and add-on factors; rentable square footage)

q: A building's replacement cost new is $520,000, and its total economic life is 40 years. Using straight-line depreciation, how much depreciation has accrued after 9 years?
explanation: Annual depreciation = $520,000 ÷ 40 = $13,000 (2.5% a year); after 9 years, $13,000 × 9 = $117,000 (22.5%). Trap: $403,000 is the depreciated value that remains, not the accrued depreciation, and $46,800 treats 9 years as 9%.
citation: Cost approach (straight-line/age-life depreciation); DOS Salesperson Syllabus Subject 8 and Subject 10 (depreciation)

q: A house is 20 years old, but extensive renovations give it an effective age of 15 years. Its total economic life is 60 years, and its replacement cost new is $480,000. Using straight-line (age-life) depreciation, what is the accrued depreciation?
explanation: Age-life depreciation uses effective age: 15 ÷ 60 = 25%; 25% × $480,000 = $120,000. Trap: using the 20-year actual age gives $160,000, and $360,000 reflects the 45 years of remaining life rather than depreciation already accrued.
citation: Cost approach (effective age; economic life); DOS Salesperson Syllabus Subject 8 (depreciation)

q: An investor buys a small office building for $1,250,000, with $275,000 of the price allocated to land. After 8 full years of straight-line cost recovery over 39 years (ignoring the mid-month convention and any improvements), what is the property's adjusted basis?
explanation: Annual deduction = ($1,250,000 − $275,000) ÷ 39 = $975,000 ÷ 39 = $25,000; 8 years = $200,000; adjusted basis = $1,250,000 − $200,000 = $1,050,000. Trap: land stays in the basis even though it is not depreciated, so $775,000 ($975,000 − $200,000) wrongly drops it; $1,250,000 ignores the depreciation, and the 27.5-year residential period gives $966,364.
citation: IRC § 168(c) (39-year nonresidential real property); IRC § 1016 (adjustments to basis); DOS Salesperson Syllabus Subject 17

q: A condominium worth $400,000 lost 20% of its value in one year and then gained 20% the next year. What is it worth now?
explanation: After the loss: $400,000 × 0.80 = $320,000; after the gain: $320,000 × 1.20 = $384,000. Trap: equal percentage changes do not cancel, because the 20% gain is figured on the smaller $320,000 base, so $400,000 is wrong.
citation: DOS Salesperson Syllabus Subject 10 (appreciation and depreciation)

q: A home bought 5 years ago for $320,000 is now worth $400,000. Using simple (straight-line) appreciation, what has been its average annual rate of appreciation?
explanation: Total appreciation = ($400,000 − $320,000) ÷ $320,000 = $80,000 ÷ $320,000 = 25%; 25% ÷ 5 years = 5% per year. Trap: dividing by the current value (20% ÷ 5 = 4%) uses the wrong base, and 25% is the total change, not the annual rate.
citation: DOS Salesperson Syllabus Subject 10 (appreciation and depreciation)

q: A house sold for $468,000, which was 20% more than the seller paid for it. What did the seller pay?
explanation: Sale price = cost × 1.20, so cost = $468,000 ÷ 1.20 = $390,000 (check: $390,000 × 1.20 = $468,000). Trap: subtracting 20% of the sale price ($374,400) uses the wrong base, because the 20% was figured on the cost.
citation: DOS Salesperson Syllabus Subject 10 (percentages)

q: An investor bought a house for $250,000 and spent $50,000 on renovations. She sold it for $360,000, paying a 5% commission and $6,000 of other selling costs. What was her profit as a percentage of her total investment?
explanation: Net proceeds = $360,000 − $18,000 commission − $6,000 = $336,000; total investment = $250,000 + $50,000 = $300,000; profit = $36,000 ÷ $300,000 = 12%. Trap: ignoring selling costs gives 20% ($60,000 ÷ $300,000), and dividing the profit by the sale price gives 10%.
citation: DOS Salesperson Syllabus Subject 10 (percentages)

q: An investor sold two properties for $120,000 each. She made a 20% profit on her cost for one and took a 20% loss on her cost for the other. What was her overall result?
explanation: Cost of the first = $120,000 ÷ 1.20 = $100,000 (a $20,000 gain); cost of the second = $120,000 ÷ 0.80 = $150,000 (a $30,000 loss); net = $20,000 − $30,000 = a $10,000 loss. Trap: the two 20% figures apply to different cost bases, so they do not offset.
citation: DOS Salesperson Syllabus Subject 10 (percentages)

q: In the cost approach, a 2,400-sq-ft house costs $225 per square foot to replace, and its detached 480-sq-ft garage costs $70 per square foot. Accrued depreciation on the buildings is $95,000, site improvements contribute $18,000, and the land is valued at $140,000. What is the indicated value?
explanation: Replacement cost = (2,400 × $225) + (480 × $70) = $540,000 + $33,600 = $573,600; less $95,000 depreciation = $478,600; plus site improvements $18,000 and land $140,000 = $636,600. Trap: pricing the garage at the house rate gives $711,000, and skipping depreciation gives $731,600.
citation: Cost approach (land + cost new − accrued depreciation); DOS Salesperson Syllabus Subject 8

q: A property sold for $520,000. The building's replacement cost new is estimated at $450,000, and it has 20% accrued depreciation. What land value does the sale indicate?
explanation: Depreciated building = $450,000 × (1 − 0.20) = $360,000; land = sale price − depreciated building = $520,000 − $360,000 = $160,000. Trap: subtracting the undepreciated cost gives $70,000, and $430,000 subtracts only the $90,000 of depreciation.
citation: Cost approach / site valuation (extraction); DOS Salesperson Syllabus Subject 8

q: In a cost approach, replacement cost new is $600,000. The appraiser finds physical deterioration of $72,000, functional obsolescence of $25,000, and external obsolescence of $18,000. The land is valued at $175,000. What is the indicated value?
explanation: Total accrued depreciation = $72,000 + $25,000 + $18,000 = $115,000; depreciated improvements = $600,000 − $115,000 = $485,000; plus land $175,000 = $660,000. Trap: all three forms are deducted, so subtracting only physical deterioration ($703,000) or skipping external obsolescence ($678,000) overstates value, and $485,000 omits the land.
citation: Cost approach (physical, functional, external depreciation); DOS Salesperson Syllabus Subject 8
